title: Coroner's report into Mississauga man's death sheds light on final interactions with Peel police
article: Two documents obtained by the Mississauga News have shed light on Clive Mensah's final moments following an interaction with Peel police on Nov. 20, 2019.

A report of postmortem by the Ontario Forensic Pathology Service and a coroner's investigation statement from the Office of the Chief Coroner were supplied by Kastner Lam, the firm representing the Mensah family.

The 24-page forensic pathology report, which includes information from one police witness's account of the incident, makes note of the 30-year-old Mississauga man's state of health after three Peel Police officers responded to his home, following receipt of a noise complaint on Nov. 20, 2019.
According to the report, police located Mensah outside of the residence, "flailing his arms and making unintelligible noises."

At approximately 3:26 a.m., officers followed Mensah into the backyard of the home on Runningbrook Drive. That's where, according to the forensic pathology report, officers gave Mensah a verbal warning to lay down on the ground and place his hands behind his back. The report indicates Mensah complied and laid face down on the deck.
"He was described to continue to fail his arms and did not put them behind his back," reads the report.
After this, the report confirms one officer deployed a Taser at Mensah, who promptly "got up off the ground." His behaviour was described as "erratic."
The report confirmed Mensah never spoke throughout the interaction.

While Mensah stood up and "advanced towards the interviewed subject officer," the report states a Taser was deployed a second time, resulting in Mensah falling face down on the grass and to go "rigid."

Though the report said the officers described Mensah as continuing to be "aggressive and combative," it goes on to explain that all three officers attempted to hold and control the man's arms and legs while he was on the grass. A Taser was deployed a third time and pepper spray was deployed to the back of Mensah's head in an effort to control him.
After this, officers were "able to handcuff him with his hands behind his back," read the report.
The report describes that Mensah "suddenly" stopped moving and became quiet. Minutes after this, a fourth officer arrived on scene and Mensah was turned over to initiate chest compressions.
At the time, one of the officers described Mensah as clearly being unresponsive, according to the forensic pathology report.
Once Mensah's body was turned over while still handcuffed, a "foamy substance" was seen around his mouth and that "agonal breathing efforts were reported."
Once paramedics arrived on scene, Mensah was identified to be without vital signs and taken to hospital where "resuscitation efforts were terminated."
Mensah was pronounced dead at 4:19 a.m. less than one hour after officers arrived on scene.
In total, Mensah had been hit shocked six times, though the report notes the Tasers were not strong enough to kill him alone.

A combination of being in an "agitated state" while interacting with police, "including blunt injuries, his restraint, his prone position in the context of morbid obesity" and the deployment of Tasers and pepper spray, ultimately led to the man's death, read the report.

Mensah's family insists Clive, who was six-foot-three and around 334 lb, was experiencing a crisis when officers responded. The man lived with schizophrenia and had a "history of psychosis," according to the forensic pathology report.
On Dec. 22, the province's Special Investigations Unit (SIU) said they are still investigating the Mississauga man's death and pursuing "additional inquires" after receiving copies of the report.
Three subject officers and two witness officers have been designated in the investigation.
Monica Hudon, SIU spokesperson, confirmed one subject officer submitted their notes and was interviewed by the SIU. The two other officers declined to be interviewed and didn't provide their notes.

"Pursuant to legislation, subject officers cannot be legally compelled to present themselves for an interview with the SIU and they do not have to submit their notes to the SIU," said Hudon, in an email.
Peel police Const. Sarah Patten said police could not comment on the case, citing the ongoing SIU investigation.
In a statement provided by Kastner Lam, the Mensah family said learning about the reports made them question why police restrained and Tasered Clive, even though he was complying.
"He didn't do anything wrong; he was no threat to anyone," said the family in a statement. "There was no reason for the police officers to advance on him, use Tasers, pepper spray and restrain him."
